Get started with MMSpower

Source: vignettes/MMSpower.Rmd
MMSpower.Rmd
library(MMSpower)

MMSpower answers four common questions in malaria molecular surveillance studies. For most, a design function says how many samples are needed, and a matching analysis function says what the data show. Every function allows for an imperfect diagnostic test (sensitivity, and specificity where it applies) and for clustered sampling across sites (icc, with n_sites or n_per_site).

This page is a short tour. Each function’s reference page explains its methods and formulas in full.

Estimating prevalence

How many people are needed to estimate a prevalence of around 30% to within ±5 percentage points, with 10 people per site and an ICC of 0.05?

des <- design_precision(prevalence = 0.3, moe = 0.05, n_per_site = 10, icc = 0.05)
des
#> $n
#> [1] 500
#> 
#> $n_sites
#> [1] 50
#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> [1] 10
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1.45
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 341
#> 
#> $moe
#> [1] 0.04965355

Once the data are in, estimate the prevalence and its confidence interval (here, 3 positives at each of the 50 sites):

estimate_prevalence(x = rep(3, des$n_sites), n = rep(10, des$n_sites), icc = 0.05)
#> $prevalence
#> [1] 0.3
#> 
#> $ci_lower
#> [1] 0.2520834
#> 
#> $ci_upper
#> [1] 0.3513905
#> 
#> $moe
#> [1] 0.04965355
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 344.8276
#> 
#> $icc
#> [1] 0.05
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1.45
#> 
#> $df
#> [1] Inf

Testing against a threshold

How many people are needed to show that prevalence is above a 5% threshold when it is really 10%, with 80% power?

design_threshold(threshold = 0.05, prevalence = 0.10)
#> $n
#> [1] 191
#> 
#> $n_sites
#> NULL
#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> NULL
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 191
#> 
#> $power
#> [1] 0.8053581

Then test the data against the threshold:

test_threshold(x = 18, n = 191, threshold = 0.05)
#> $p_value
#> [1] 0.007726515
#> 
#> $reject
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $prevalence
#> [1] 0.09424084
#> 
#> $ci_lower
#> [1] 0.06179912
#> 
#> $ci_upper
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 191
#> 
#> $icc
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $df
#> [1] Inf

Detecting a rare variant

How many people are needed for an 80% chance of finding at least one case of a variant present in 1% of infections?

design_detection(prevalence = 0.01)
#> $n
#> [1] 161
#> 
#> $n_sites
#> NULL
#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> NULL
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 161
#> 
#> $detection_prob
#> [1] 0.8017257

Comparing two groups

How many people per group are needed to detect a difference between 10% and 20% prevalence, with 30 sites per group and an ICC of 0.02?

design_difference(prevalence1 = 0.10, prevalence2 = 0.20, n_sites1 = 30, icc = 0.02)
#> $n_per_group
#> [1] 240 240
#> 
#> $n
#> [1] 480
#> 
#> $n_sites
#> [1] 30 30
#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> [1] 8 8
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1.14 1.14
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 199 199
#> 
#> $power
#> [1] 0.82185

Then test for a difference:

test_difference(x1 = 24, n1 = 240, x2 = 48, n2 = 240, icc = 0.02)
#> $difference
#> [1] -0.1
#> 
#> $ci_lower
#> [1] -0.2611286
#> 
#> $ci_upper
#> [1] 0.05779169
#> 
#> $p_value
#> [1] 0.2019338
#> 
#> $reject
#> [1] FALSE
#> 
#> $prevalence1
#> [1] 0.1
#> 
#> $prevalence2
#> [1] 0.2
#> 
#> $n_eff1
#> [1] 41.52249
#> 
#> $n_eff2
#> [1] 41.52249
#> 
#> $icc1
#> [1] 0.02
#> 
#> $icc2
#> [1] 0.02
#> 
#> $deff1
#> [1] 5.78
#> 
#> $deff2
#> [1] 5.78
#> 
#> $df
#> [1] Inf

Costing a study

Finally, cost a design from its sample size and number of sites. The design’s n is the number of samples sequenced; here each costs 50 in all:

estimate_cost(n_sequenced = des$n, cost_per_sequenced = 50, n_sites = des$n_sites,
              fixed_cost_per_site = 500, transport_cost_per_site = 200)
#> $total_cost
#> [1] 60000
#> 
#> $variable_cost
#> [1] 25000
#> 
#> $stage_cost
#>  screened collected sequenced 
#>         0         0     25000 
#> 
#> $site_cost
#> [1] 35000
#> 
#> $budget_remaining
#> NULL

estimate_cost() can also cost screening and sample collection as separate stages; see the Costing a study tutorial.
